skyline.text: Müller’s test for a populist, and the rest who don’t count
Ajay Shah on the machinery of the modern populist
How Poland’s elite was murdered, name by name

footnote.text: It’s only words and words are all we have.

brief.head: Four magic terms
brief.text: Say market failure, public good, adverse selection and moral hazard correctly, Ajay Shah said, “then basically you’re an economist”. Every field borrows common words for its own meanings. {042-C01}

brief.head: Follow the tribe
brief.text: Within eight years, Amit Varma said, Donald Trump turned the Republican Party against much of what it stood for. Many people, he concluded, hold principles only because their tribe does. {042-C10}

brief.head: Hollow parties
brief.text: Parties need to be institutions too, Ajay Shah argued, not the iron hand of one or two people. The gutting of the Republicans will matter for 25 years. {042-C11}

brief.head: Democracy, plus two
brief.text: People having power is “a damn good thing”, Amit Varma said. But it also needs a republic that protects individual rights, and a healthy public discourse where simplistic narratives lose. {042-C16}

brief.head: Keeping score
brief.text: Rival democracy measures disagree somewhat but agree quite a bit, Ajay Shah said. He reads Freedom House for ease of use; V-Dem, he thinks, is better but more work. {042-R12}

thought.text: Every generation has to fight its own battles.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, after Amit Varma invoked Jefferson’s eternal vigilance over Hungary

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what populism really means
lead.head: Not popular, just populist
body: Amit Varma opened the episode holding a leaf, which he introduced as an ancient manuscript bearing mysterious words in a mysterious language. The word the hosts set out to decode was one everybody uses: populism.
“I’m just a clueless economist,” Ajay Shah confessed. For years he had thought populism meant something like popular. “And what’s wrong with popular?”
Varma had already given the answer. Populism is not what is popular: in the sense political scientists use it, it is toxic.
Neither host claimed to be an expert. But both, Varma said, have skin in the game, and Shah called 2024 “a really important year” in the journey of populism.
## The checklist
Their guide was Jan-Werner Müller’s *What Is Populism?*, which lists seven things that populists have in common.
The core claim, Varma said, is that “only some of the people are the people”. Populists treat their supporters as the people and everyone else as illegitimate. {042-C02}

The rest of the list follows: anti-elite rhetoric, majorities that “act like mistreated minorities”, parties that turn into personality cults, a show of being one of the people, simplistic narratives and, growing out of them all, conspiracy theories.
Varma’s favourite of the seven is the simplistic narrative. The world is so complex, he said, that “simple stories are a feature, not a bug for the normal person”. {042-C05}
Tell unemployed workers that their jobs went overseas and immigrants took the rest, and the story appears to explain the world. It also supplies someone to rail against.
Hatred, Shah added, is a simplistic narrative that appeals to emotion. “Great leaders make us better than who we are,” he said. Populist leaders “bring out the worst in us”.
Varma added a corrective for the elites: when people vote against your values, “something is wrong with you and your message”.
## Power, and how to keep it
Once populists win, Varma said, they need “an additional playbook” to make sure they don’t lose power: colonise the state, reward clients and silence civil society. {042-C12}
Shah’s Roman shorthand for the result was bread and circus: handouts to placate people, and a drumbeat of noise to keep them from thinking.

He then toured four countries he follows. In America, Donald Trump’s own agencies refused to torment his rivals. In Israel, people from elite military formations led protests in defence of the judges. Hungary has turned thuggish despite being in the European Union.

Poland was the story of redemption. After ten years under the Law and Justice Party, the centre-left party led by Donald Tusk won in October 2023. Now it must undo the damage without breaking the rule of law. {042-S08}
## What is new
What is different this time, Varma argued, is social media, whose incentives pull everyone towards the extremes. {042-C18}
Shah blamed social media for a counterfeit of knowledge, in which clueless people around the dinner table comfortably mouth truths. He saw no way out “other than our striving”.
Varma closed with a word for listeners far from these countries. “We all have skin in the game,” he said. “This matters to all of us.”

second.label: Rich and unafraid
second.head: Money talks back
second.deck: Ajay Shah reads America’s institutions in one billionaire’s nerve
body: Rich people could be the most timid of all, Ajay Shah said, because they have the most to lose and “you just don’t want to mess with the government”. Whether they feel safe to speak up says something about a country. {042-S02}

In the United States, Jeff Bezos, the richest person in the country, openly staked out an anti-Trump position. He also owned the *Washington Post*, one of the newspapers that exposed the misdeeds of the Trump years. “Again, I say, wow,” Shah said.

Amit Varma, who counts Bezos among his heroes, added that under him the *Post* kept running anti-Amazon and anti-Bezos stories. {#post} Strong institutions, he said, breed values that become part of the culture.

quote.text: So in a way, rich people have hostages. They have the most to lose.

second.caption: the billionaire who spoke up

third.head: Slowly, the picture loads
body: Amit Varma remembers downloading photographs over a dial-up connection in the 1990s, “of Samantha Fox or otherwise”. First came a pixelated blur. Then, gradually, the picture sharpened into high definition. {042-J07}
“Whatever the objectives,” he said, “you get a thrill that you can see clearly.” Ideas, he said, can feel exactly the same way.

He too had once thought populism was something like popular, as, he said, everybody does at first. Then reading supplied what he calls frames of seeing, and the blurry picture came into focus. {042-S10}
“I just find that that’s so beautiful and miraculous,” he said, “that we can actually do that and make ourselves see better.” What the hosts had laid out, he said, helped him see the world better.
third.caption: ideas that load like old photographs

p2.title: The populist playbook
p2.deck: Jan-Werner Müller’s checklist, how populists keep power, and four countries where the drama is playing out

sections.label: Seven traits
sections.head: We the people (terms apply)
sections.caption: Müller’s seven-point checklist
body: Jan-Werner Müller, Amit Varma said, finds seven things that populists have in common. First, they define the people as those who support them. Donald Trump, he said, once declared that the other people don’t matter. {042-C02}
Ajay Shah added that Trump calls the press “the enemies of the people”. In the same spirit, Varma said, supporters become patriots and critics anti-national.

The second trait is anti-elite rhetoric; the third, playing the victim. Müller says that “majorities act like mistreated minorities”, and Shah added that populists dig up some grievance from 500 or 50 years ago and exaggerate it. {042-C03}
## The useful enemy

The German theorist Carl Schmitt, Varma said, held that what is essential to politics is having an enemy. With no invader to rally against, populists find enemies within, and pose as outsiders while being hardcore insiders. Trump, he said, has been a crony capitalist for forty years. {042-C04}

Fourth, populist parties become personality cults. Fifth, the leader claims to be one of the people. Shah pointed to Trump’s photo ops eating junk food. Some hamburgers are tasty, Varma conceded, but if you say a hamburger is good for you, “there’s a serious kind of problem with that”.
Sixth come simplistic narratives; seventh, conspiracy theories, which grow out of populism’s own logic.
~ Varma ended the list with an old line: “Religion is the opiate of the masses.” Shah had a sequel ready: “Conspiracy theories are the opiate of the asses.” {042-J01}

quote.text: The core claim of populism is that only some of the people are the people.

sections.label: Left and right
sections.head: Two wings, one poison
sections.caption: populism of the left and the right
body: Populism, Ajay Shah said, is not about the old classification of left and right. Hitler, Mao, Lenin and Donald Trump were all populists, in very different political systems, and populism of the left is as toxic as populism of the right.

Amit Varma’s preferred lens is another binary: freedom against authoritarianism, consent against coercion. By that test, he said, every party in India is left on economics, right on social issues and statist throughout. {042-C07}

Shah sees the central engine of populism as rousing the underclass to hate the elite. A movement stokes anger against the cultural, business and intellectual elites, commands the state, and then puts “the knife into the other three”. {042-C08}
## A word worth saving
Shah used the word elite deliberately, he said, “because I want to torment the wokes in the audience as well”. All the great truth, beauty and wealth creation, he argued, is done by elites. {042-J04}

Varma agreed that anti-elitism becomes anti-knowledge, leaving leaders to take advice from quacks. But elites are often complacent, entitled and condescending, he said, and when people vote against your values, something is wrong with you and your message, not with the people. {042-C09}
~ Shah traced the danger back to Plato’s *Republic*, clear-eyed about democracy, and forward through Mussolini’s radio, Hitler’s rallies, television and now social media. {042-R10}

quote.text: It is consent and coercion. That is a binary.

sections.label: Holding power
sections.head: Colonise, reward, silence
sections.caption: how populists keep power
body: Winning power takes one playbook, Amit Varma said; keeping it takes another. Jan-Werner Müller describes three moves that populist regimes have in common. {042-C12}

First, they colonise the state, putting their own people in charge of independent institutions and discrediting the rest. It can be done by brute force or slowly. Varma reached for the parable of the frog in boiling water, then debunked it: the frog will at some point jump out. “But it’s a great metaphor.” {042-J12}

Second comes mass clientelism: contracts, favours and protection from competition, especially foreign competition. Ajay Shah added subsidy programmes, a crude form of political clientelism that has become so normal nobody notices.
## The Roman recipe

Shah borrowed a phrase from Roman history: bread and circus. Bread mollifies people with subsidies and transfers. The circus, once gladiators in the Colosseum, is today the noise on TV and social media. {042-C14}
Third, populists shut down dissent in civil society, often starting with NGOs. They need not jail everyone, Varma said. Make an example of a couple of people and the rest fall silent. {042-C13}
~ Shah saw this as part of monopolising every organisation in society. In China, he said, there is a communist party group inside every company. {#china}

quote.text: They don’t even realize why they are silent. They may not even think they’re silent.

sections.label: United States
sections.head: When the taxman said no
sections.caption: Trump and America’s institutions
body: Ajay Shah’s first stop was the United States, where Donald Trump has taken the Republican Party far into populism. What Shah found remarkable was that in office, Trump could not subvert the institutions to any significant extent.
Trump asked the IRS and the FBI to investigate and torment his rivals. By and large, they refused. In Shah’s telling, they said: “No, this is not legal. This violates our rules.” {042-S01}
Nor could Trump stop the Democrats from raising money, hiring advisors, rallying in the streets and getting out the vote in 2020.
## More than a fair count

That, Shah argued, is what a free and fair election needs. Correct counting is not enough. Opposition parties must be able to fundraise, use a free press and organise without fear of the state’s coercive arms. {042-C15}
The right test, he said, is how many percentage points of vote share state pressure on the opposition shifts.
Even so, Shah was blown away by how small the margin was: Biden just squeaked through. With the cases against Trump not played through in time, he said, Trump remains viable in 2024.
~ Amit Varma agreed. Votes, he believes, are by and large counted correctly in India. {#counted} What matters is whether parties are free to campaign and people free to speak their minds.

quote.text: And by and large, they refused to do so. Can you think about that? How marvelous is that?

sections.label: Hungary and Poland
sections.head: The star pupil comes back
sections.caption: Hungary’s slide and Poland’s return
body: Hungary, Ajay Shah said, is the country of John von Neumann, and after communism it was expected to do as well as Czechoslovakia. Instead it became a thuggish right-wing state, despite membership of the European Union and NATO. {042-S05}
Elections still happen, but police go after the opposition, the press is gone and the Central European University was driven out. Viktor Orbán has won five times. {#orban}
## Poland’s second chance

Poland rebuilt quickly after 1989. Around 2005 its nation builders told Shah that the EU gave them “a rough working draft” of what a law or an institution looks like. {042-S07} Inside the EU and NATO, Poland took off; Ukraine, outside them, did not.

Then came ten years of the Law and Justice Party, “an alliance between farmers and Christians and thugs”, in Shah’s words. At the October 2023 election, Poland’s Freedom House score stood at 80 out of 100, against Hungary’s 65. {#poland80}
In that election, the centre-left party led by Donald Tusk won. The task now is to undo the damage while respecting due process.
~ Amit Varma had a T-shirt line ready: “You are my Poland.” He imagined the genteel Shah burning trucks and beating people up, and hoped he too could be brought back. {042-J05}

quote.text: So you can’t just send the police and grab the chief justice.

sections.label: Social media
sections.head: Wired for the extremes
sections.caption: social media and the extremes
body: History may not repeat, but it rhymes, Amit Varma said. What is new this time is the pace of technological change and the incentives social media has created. {042-J14}

Someone joins Twitter, he said, wanting a sense of community, and joins an ideological tribe. Status there comes from signalling, attacking the other side and cancelling insiders who are not pure enough. A vocal minority drags discourse to the extremes, even if the silent majority is not like this. {042-C18}
In 2016 he wondered how the median voter theorem had broken. It predicted near-identical centrist candidates, such as Jeb Bush and Hillary Clinton. Then Donald Trump won the general election.
## Groups, not people

The left is swinging the same way. “Wokeism begins where liberalism ends,” Varma said. Liberalism is about each person, who contains multitudes; wokeism thinks only in groups, with a ready-made story of victimhood or oppression. {042-C19}
Ajay Shah answered with a poet’s question, “What happened to the post-war dream?”, and his own reply: social media.
~ It creates, Shah said, “a vulgar familiarity”, in which 140 characters pass for knowledge. {042-C20} In his father’s world, people would say they had only read four books on a subject.

quote.text: When I think of the incentives of social media, I think the incentive everywhere is towards the extremes.

side.boxText: Amit Varma calls Jan-Werner Müller’s *What Is Populism?* the book that taught him a lot about populism, one everyone should read. He wrote a column on it long ago. It lists seven things that populists have in common. {042-R01}

contQuote.text: Even if the people vote in someone who does not align with your values, that doesn’t mean something is wrong with the people. It means something is wrong with you and your message.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A war for a soul, a murderous list, and tears in Warsaw

stories.caption: the war for Israel’s soul
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, a declared admirer, on a country at a crossroads
stories.head: Soldiers march for the judges
body: Ajay Shah put his biases on the table first. He is deeply sympathetic to the project of Israel, a country that, he said, came out of nothing and a war in 1948 and built one of the world’s great countries. {#israel1948}
As a sign of its decency, he noted that gay people cross illegally into Israel every day from neighbouring Arab countries, because homosexuality is legal there.

But after the fall of the USSR, a large wave of Jewish immigrants arrived from Eastern Europe, most notably Russia, with conservative values on religion, women and personal freedom. “So there is a war for the soul of Israel that is afoot,” Shah said. {042-S03}
It came to a head when Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s leader, tried to give the executive a veto over the selection of judges.

People poured into the streets, and again and again the movement was led by people from elite military formations. Their message, as Shah put it: “Look, we are soldiers, we have given our life and our blood to protect this country. But we do not believe that the executive branch should ride roughshod over the judicial branch.” {042-S04}

Military people, Shah said, are often the first to sign on to the destruction of institutions. In Israel they championed the separation of powers, and won about 75 per cent, though not 100 per cent, of what they fought for.
~ Then came the Hamas disaster, for which Shah faults Netanyahu and the executive. The soul of Israel, he said, is up for grabs.
stories.why: In Shah’s account, a democracy’s character rests on the values its citizens carry. Change who the citizens are and the politics can turn, and even one of the world’s great success stories can slide back into the battles of the twentieth century.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma said the battle for Israel’s soul was news to him, and something he would be following.

stories.start: It for centuries has been savaged by one monstrous country on one side, Germany
stories.end: building an anti-communist movement with Lek Hwalesa organizing the portworkers of Poland
stories.caption: Stalin’s list
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Poland lost its elite
stories.head: Forty thousand names
body: Poland, Ajay Shah said, was savaged for centuries by monstrous neighbours on either side. On 1 September 1939 Nazi Germany invaded; on 16 September, the Russians followed. {#invaded}
After the Second World War the Russians swallowed Poland and installed a communist party. Stalin took care to draw up a list of 40,000 people of the Polish elite, and they were murdered. {042-S06}

Shah asked listeners to pause and think of any country they love. “Imagine a carefully made list of the forty thousand people who make up the intellectual and the business and the cultural elite of the country. And imagine that they get murdered.”
~ That is where modern Poland began, he said. Yet it was among the first to build an anti-communist movement, with Lech Walesa organising its port workers.
stories.why: Culture is transmitted by people, Shah said, and those 40,000 were disproportionately important carriers of knowledge, values and norms. Losing them is like destroying the foundations of a country, and rebuilding takes generations.

stories.caption: three days in Warsaw
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on history and the art of travel
stories.head: Tears on the tourist trail
body: For people who read history, Ajay Shah said, there are few things more moving than visiting Poland. He once spent three days visiting sites in Warsaw, “just weeping like a baby”. {#warsaw}
Amit Varma, thinking aloud, said the story of any place is also a story of human civilisation, and Poland stood at the centre of so much of the last century’s turmoil.
A tourist who arrives without any impressions will see buildings and streets and notice the weather, he said. But the deeper you go, the more everything suddenly has meaning and significance.

~ Shah had the last word. “The magic of travel is the child of learning culture, learning history. Then travel comes alive.” Otherwise, he said, you are just sightseeing, and might as well go to the beach in Goa. {042-S09}
stories.why: Knowing a place’s history turns sightseeing into an encounter with human civilisation. For both hosts, the reading done before a journey is what gives the buildings and streets of a city their meaning.

stories.start: I'll take a brief digression, though, is related and uh gentle reader
stories.end: that I'm not going to make any further comment on it
stories.caption: Hamas, Israel and staying silent
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why the hosts stayed out of a war
stories.head: Nuance draws fire from both sides
body: After the Hamas attacks and Israel’s retaliation, listeners asked the hosts to discuss the war. They declined, Amit Varma said, because they did not have enough knowledge of something so complex.

He still set out what he called a nuanced position. He is against Hamas, which he called evil, and against the Israeli state as it currently is. {#position} He cares deeply for the Palestinian people and sympathises with the Israeli people.

Even that, he said, gets you attacked, because everything is black and white. “If you speak against Israel, it is assumed you are anti-Semitic, which is daft. If you speak against Hamas, it is assumed that you’re against the Palestinian people, which is daft.” {042-S11}
~ Hamas, in his opinion, is the worst thing that happened to Palestine. Beyond that, he said, he knew too little to comment.

quote.text: I am with the people on both sides.

quiz.a: William Golding’s *Lord of the Flies*, where people bully and torment each other.
